title: Is AI Impacting Global Labor Markets? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. As companies integrate artificial intelligence (AI) tools into their operations, the effects on hiring are starting to show up in the economic data for some industries and workers around the world, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The timing and extent of AI’s impact on job markets depend on the rate of adoption among companies. However, there are inconsistencies in surveys about AI adoption, leading to results that often vary widely. To overcome this, our economists compiled 11 different surveys that measure AI adoption across countries and applied a statistical algorithm to extract rankings, write Goldman Sachs Research economist Sarah Dong and Joseph Briggs, who leads the Global Economics team, in a report. After rescaling around the OECD’s adoption survey­—the most globally comprehensive measure in our economists’ compiled data—Goldman Sachs Research finds that major developed markets are ahead of other countries in deploying AI, with adoption rates between 15%–20%. Among developed markets, France, the US, the Netherlands, and the UK score at the top end of this range of AI adoption. In major emerging markets, adoption rates are in the range of 10%–15%, according to Goldman Sachs Research estimates. Our economists also find that industries with greater exposure to AI automation have been associated with slower growth in job openings since the second half of 2022. The relationship between exposure to AI and slower growth in job openings was more pronounced in Germany, Australia, and the US. “This cross-industry result confirms our prior finding that the onset of generative AI tools may have led companies in highly exposed industries to re-evaluate their hiring plans,” Dong and Briggs write. There is evidence that employment in information and communication services, two of the industries that are the most exposed to AI, has slowed because of AI, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Employment in these sectors has slowed across nearly all major developed markets since 2022. In the US, employment in those industries has fallen below its long-run trend, while it remains near or above the long-run trend in other developed countries. “These patterns suggest tech sector (broadly defined) hiring headwinds are global in nature, although outright negative impacts are most compelling in the US,” Dong and Briggs write. Beyond information and communication services, an assessment of other industries with high exposure to AI reveals a similar, albeit more muted, pattern of AI-related employment headwinds relative to the US. Employment in call centers, software publishing, management consulting, and advertising services has fallen sharply below trend across the developed world. Call center employment, for instance, now stands 39% below trend in the US, 33% below trend in Canada, and 27% below trend in Germany. “These patterns confirm that, like in the US, AI-employment headwinds are visible in industries where labor-automating tools are already available,” Dong and Briggs write. Goldman Sachs Research performed another analysis, which included AI-exposure scores in a cross-country panel for more than 800 occupations, to more rigorously test the impact of AI on employment. Our economists find that a 10% occupational exposure to AI is only associated with a 0.1 percentage point drag to annual headcount growth in France, Canada, and the US. The analysis suggests that “economy-wide hiring headwinds remain limited,” Dong and Briggs write. While AI’s overall impact on job markets appears limited, recent anecdotes and US labor market data suggest that AI displacement could be stronger among entry-level workers. Goldman Sachs Research’s analysis of occupational growth based on entry- and non-entry-level groups signals that junior workers may face greater headwinds to hiring due to AI adoption. “AI-related hiring headwinds are clearly visible in official and unofficial employment data, but impacts are limited to a narrow set of industries and workers,” Dong and Briggs write. title: Meet U of G’s First Schulich Leaders - U of G News
content: Canada’s largest undergraduate STEM scholarships support entrepreneurial-minded students Learning how to put AI to use for the greater good and helping Canadian farmers with food sustainability are the goals of two Schulich Leaders who will begin their journeys at the University of Guelph this fall. Aryan Thakur will pursue computer engineering and Matteo Volpini will study agriculture with the support of Schulich Leader Scholarships, Canada’s most prestigious STEM scholarship program. Schulich Leader Scholarships provide $100,000 for a science, technology or math degree, or $120,000 for an engineering degree, for entrepreneurial-minded students. U of G is proud to be part of the prestigious scholarship program as it’s a testament to the University’s ability to attract some of Canada’s most competitive STEM students who aspire to careers in tech, engineering and applied research. “As we celebrate 15 years of Schulich Leaders, we are proud to have supported more than 1,000 exceptional Canadian students pursuing STEM degrees at our country’s top universities,” says Judy Schulich, president, The Schulich Foundation. “Schulich Leader Scholarships help attract and retain outstanding talent, empowering the next generation of innovators and entrepreneurs. By supporting their ambition and creating the conditions for them to succeed, we can ensure their innovations drive Canada’s future prosperity.” A Schulich Leader Scholarship is life changing, says Aryan Thakur, whose interest in artificial intelligence and machine learning drew him to U of G’s Computer Engineering program in the College of Engineering. As part of a generation who grew up alongside technology, Thakur knew early on he wanted to be part of an industry revolutionizing the world. “AI and machine learning are going to provide a lot of opportunity,” he says, “and I want to align myself with that.” Eager to launch his own start-up, Thakur says his program’s co-op stream is the kind of experiential learning that will build a foundation for him, from which to grow his own ideas. He knows there is work to do in the field. AI is not yet functioning at 100%, and so he is dedicated to being part of improving it, ultimately putting it to use for good. “I want to help people,” he says, “using technology to have a meaningful impact.” Being a Schulich Leader is about more than just financial support, he says. “The ability to network with fellow Scholars really does help with job opportunities or even just aligning with others going through the same life transition.” It was while growing up on a small hobby farm learning tree pruning and how to pick cherries and peaches and apples that Matteo Volpini learned the kind of devastation disease can bring to plants and the crops of farmers. The years his family lost nearly 200 trees to disease, pests and the environment, he started researching where he could study plant science and food sustainability. What he found was the Bachelor of Science in Agriculture program at the Ontario Agricultural College. “I’m excited to learn more about gene-editing technology, gain more plant knowledge and learn how disease affects plants, how pesticides and fungicides can help prevent these things,” he says. His goals don’t end there. “I’d like to start a business dedicated to global food sustainability that supports Canadian farmers by developing resilient crop varieties that can better withstand environmental stressors like pests, disease and unpredictable weather.” As a Schulich Leader, he joins a community of STEM students with similar interests across a broad spectrum of disciplines. “It’s such a great resource to have,” he says. “There are so many opportunities to learn from each other or to collaborate.” Recognizing the increasing importance and impact that STEM disciplines have on the prosperity of future generations, businessman and philanthropist Seymour Schulich established this $200 million scholarship fund in 2012 to encourage our best and brightest students to become Schulich Leader Scholars: the next generation of entrepreneurial-minded, technology innovators. Through The Schulich Foundation and United Jewish Appeal, these prestigious entrance scholarships are awarded to 100 high school graduates enrolling in a science, technology, engineering or mathematics (STEM) undergraduate program at 20 partner universities in Canada. Every high school in Canada can submit one Schulich Leader Nominee per academic year based entrepreneurial leadership and financial need.

content: Grammy-winning Colombian recording artist Karol G has officially released her sixth full-length studio project, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto. The the 14-track collection stands out for its star-studded guest list, headlined by long-awaited collaborations with Drake on the track “Ahí” and Bruno Mars on the R&B-infused ballad “Still“. Additional features across the record include Cigarettes After Sex frontman Greg Gonzalez on “Después de Ti,” alongside rising Spanish vocalists Judeline and Rusowsky on “Bby Wow”. Moving away from the energetic, tropical rhythms that defined her 2025 release Tropicoqueta, the new material explores vulnerability, emotional recovery, and nostalgia. During a recent concert at Toronto’s Rogers Stadium where she initially announced the project, the performer explained that the album “opens a door for my fans to a more intimate Carolina.” Inspiration for the record began taking shape during solo trips through Hawaii, where the singer reflected on the isolation that can accompany fame. Production was handled primarily in low-lit studio sessions featuring frequent collaborator Ovy on the Drums alongside producers Tainy, Cashmere Cat, and KEITYN. The release coincides directly with the ongoing North American leg of Karol’s Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, following record-breaking stadium performances. Following scheduled stops in Las Vegas, the tour is slated to cross North America, Mexico, South America, and Europe through mid-2027. Editorial credit: Geoffrey Clowes / Shutterstock.com

title: GS Caltex Tightens Defense, Eyes Consecutive Title - 조선일보
content: Defending champions diversify attacks, add Tanacha to reduce Silva's burden after historic win [Cheongpyeong=Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "Through an unexpected championship that no one anticipated, the players have grown significantly. The team has become more solid overall." The 'underdog' achieved a historic championship. Now, they are aiming for a second consecutive title. GS Caltex defied all expectations in the 2025-2026 season, securing third place in the regular season. In the postseason, they achieved six consecutive wins against Heungkuk Life, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, and Korea Expressway Corporation, clinching the championship trophy. This marked the team's first title in six years since the 2020-2021 season. At Cheongpyeong GS Caltex, head coach Lee Young-Taek, discussing preparations for the new season, said, "Although we won the championship, we aimed to bring changes to the team's strength. With Tanacha's addition, we could reduce Silva's burden, and it was impressive to see our players grow even further," expressing pride. "He floated in the air for two days after winning. Now that the new season is approaching, I feel the surrounding expectations. The pressure has definitely increased," he sighed. However, he emphasized, "It became an opportunity to understand how to win championships. The team atmosphere, unity, and focus were excellent. The players themselves know what kind of volleyball they should play, and my task as a coach is to bring that out on the court." Ultimately, GS Caltex's challenge is to reduce reliance on 'queen' Gyselle Silva's attacks. Even after last season's victory, they couldn't avoid criticism like 'ultimately a one-woman Silva championship' and 'Gyselle Silva Caltex.' Silva recorded 1,005 points, 1,008 points, and 1,083 points over three years in Korea, achieving the remarkable feat of scoring over 1,000 points for three consecutive years. However, Silva, born in 1991, is at an age where each year brings significant change. Coach Lee Young-Taek stated, "Scoring over 1,000 points is proof of Silva's consistent outstanding performance, so it's not bad. Still, I want to lessen Silva's attacking burden. This year, we have high expectations for the Asian quota player Tanacha. We aim to demonstrate more diverse attack distribution and ideal volleyball this year." After the championship, the team had a quiet off-season. Compared to the previous season, only the Asian quota player changed from Reina Tokoku to Tanacha Sooksom. Tanacha is in her fourth season in Korea. She is praised for her exceptional stamina and attacking skills and has quickly adapted to GS Caltex. Additionally, the team recruited two Japanese coaches: Kawamura Shinji and Ishii Sugurou. Coach Kawamura has been acquainted with Lee Young-Taek since his playing days and has experience as a coach in the Japanese league. Coach Sugurou is responsible for guiding GS Caltex's young setters: Kim Ji-won, Lee Yoon-shin, and Choi Yoon-young. If Silva and Tanacha are fixed, the remaining wing position is for one outside hitter. Fierce competition is expected among Yoo Seo-yeon, Kwon Min-ji, Lee Ju-a, Kim Ju-hyang, and Kim Mi-yeon. The head coach emphasized, "These are players with strong individuality. There will be timing when bold changes are needed during games. Other players must support Silva well. Now is the time for competition. I hope they show the roles they can play." For middle blockers, Oh Se-yeon has solidified her position, leaving one remaining spot contested between Choi Ga-eun and Choi Yu-rim. Coach Lee Young-Taek explained, "Oh Se-yeon has established herself, and her desire to perform better and win again is evident. Last season, we focused on Choi Yu-rim's growth because Choi Ga-eun was injured, but Choi Ga-eun also performed well in the latter half, with the advantage of abundant energy. We will keep both players competing until the day before the opening match." When Oh Se-yeon's name came up, Yoo Seo-yeon raised her voice: "During the championship match, I saw Seo-yeon overcoming difficulties and striving, and I thought she had become a completely different player. Her mindset had changed," she smiled brightly. The libero position is also solid with Han Soo-jin and Yoo Ga-ram, and Kim Hyo-im has significantly improved after recently returning from the national team. GS Caltex's signature net defense is expected to remain formidable this season. GS Caltex aims to become a 'consistently strong team' that continuously advances to the spring playoffs without being complacent about their past victory. When asked to predict this season's structure, the head coach's tone turned serious. He said, "Lightheartedly, I think Hyundai Engineering & Construction will continue to perform well. Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK) struggled early last season but showed strong form in the latter half. The rest will be a mix. This season will likely see many coaches with more gray hair," he laughed. "Ultimately, injury management is most important. Every team has a clear gap between starters and substitutes." "Last season's media day, we stated our goal was over 20 wins and 60 points. We achieved 19 wins and 57 points. I believe the playoff qualification is around 60 points. Once we reach the playoffs, we have Silva. We will book a hotel for the championship match in advance. We will do our best to avoid a 'no-show.'" title: Deacon Corey Lashawn Boyd GS’21, GS’26 builds a legacy of resilience, faith, and leadership - Bethel University
content: Deacon Corey Lashawn Boyd GS’21, GS’26 spent years hearing that college might not be in his future. Today, he holds two graduate degrees from Bethel University, serves as chief equity officer for the State of Minnesota, and is an ordained deacon at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church in Minneapolis. For Deacon Corey Lashawn Boyd GS’21, GS’26, every diploma he’s earned tells part of a larger story. School was challenging from the beginning. Boyd entered kindergarten without having attended preschool and struggled to adjust to the classroom. He repeated kindergarten, and by first grade, educators identified him as having a learning disability. His school days often included one-on-one instruction outside the traditional classroom, where he worked with specialists on speech, writing, reading, and other foundational skills. One teacher who left a lasting impression was Miss Berg, whose warmth and encouragement helped Boyd build confidence in school. “For every answer I got right, she gave me my reward of Goldfish crackers,” Boyd laughs. “I would work for the correct answer just to have them.” By junior high, educators told Boyd he no longer needed special education classes. He was capable of succeeding academically. He simply learned differently. Still, recognizing his ability and believing in it were two different things. “I had all these dreams and aspirations of going to college. … I never lost hope of wanting to go.” As Boyd grew older, football became a major focus. Inspired by Notre Dame quarterback Tony Rice, he dreamed of playing quarterback for the Fighting Irish. At times, academic challenges kept him from competing, but they did not erase his goal of continuing his education. “I had all these dreams and aspirations of going to college. Even though I struggled academically, I never lost hope of wanting to go,” Boyd says. Near the end of high school, Boyd was preparing to join the U.S. Marine Corps when a conversation with his pastor changed his direction. He told Rev. Walter R. Bauldrick Sr. of Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church that he wanted to attend Virginia State University. Bauldrick connected him with Jadonal Ford, a Virginia State alumnus and fellow member of the school’s chapter of Alpha Phi Alpha. Ford became an important mentor, helping Boyd navigate admission, secure funding, and stay on track. Boyd enrolled at Virginia State without ever having visited campus. Although his time there was brief, the experience strengthened his identity as a Black man and introduced him to new examples of Black achievement and leadership. That experience eventually led him back to his former high school, where he worked as a tutor, then in attendance and registration, and later as an academic advisor. “The registrar’s office is where I began to understand that young people experience more challenges prior to arriving at school than most people know,” he says. In 2018, Boyd moved to Minnesota to expand his career into equity and systems-level work. The move also opened the door to a new chapter at Bethel University. Boyd knew he wanted to work in community, support young people, and influence systems, but he was still determining what his next chapter should look like. “My wife was on board with me going back to school, but I was distracted by personal challenges I faced after leaving Evanston,” he says. As he researched universities in Minnesota, Bethel stood out. The name carried a personal connection because Boyd grew up in a church of the same name. But he also sensed God leading him specifically toward Bethel University. “I felt like God was talking to me, telling me to look at Bethel University,” Boyd says. “He was saying, ‘That’s where you’re going to grow. That’s where you’re going to find out who you are.’” Even then, doubt followed him. Boyd worried his undergraduate record would keep him from graduate school. He questioned whether he was prepared to succeed at that level. With guidance from then-enrollment counselor Erica Garrett, he completed the application and learned more about Bethel’s M.A. in Strategic Leadership program. Boyd remembers the vocational guidance and genuine warmth he experienced from Bethel staff. He recalls talking with Sam Helgerson about leadership, life, Christ, and what it meant to be a Christian leader. “That signaled a rebirth,” he says. “That was my new beginning. That was the journey of learning who I was as a leader.” Bethel’s strategic leadership program introduced Boyd to tools he continues to use, including strengths assessments that helped him better understand how he is wired professionally and develop his emotional intelligence. He says the experience also helped him understand how his Christian faith could shape the way he leads. “Strategic leadership showed me the human side, but it also showed me how to connect to Christ in the work that I do as a leader,” he says. Boyd eventually became chief equity officer for the State of Minnesota, bringing together years of experience in education, equity, leadership, and systems-level work. Boyd completed his M.A. in Strategic Leadership in 2021 during a difficult season. His mother had died that January, making this the first of his graduations she was unable to attend. After earning his master’s degree, Boyd paused to consider whether to continue his education. He had already earned a high school diploma, bachelor’s degree, and master’s degree, accomplishing what many had once told him might not be possible. His journey continued in other ways too. Prompted by his pastor, Boyd completed a nine-month preparation process and became an ordained deacon at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church in Minneapolis. Meanwhile, Professor Jeanine Parolini continued inviting him to Bethel events and leadership conversations, keeping the possibility of an MBA on his radar. Eventually, Boyd realized that returning to Bethel for a second master’s degree represented something different. His earlier degrees had often been driven by a desire to prove himself to others. Returning for his MBA became an opportunity to prove something to himself: that he belonged. Professor Kevin Johnson became another important influence, challenging Boyd’s thinking and shaping how he applies leadership principles to equity work. Boyd also credits coach Tom Christie with helping him navigate complex career choices and portfolio development. He sees those relationships as part of God’s intentional design throughout his life. “These are people that were strategically placed in my life,” Boyd says. “I love strategy because God is the ultimate chess player.” Boyd says his perspective on leadership has changed as he has grown older. He thinks less about chasing a particular job or title and focuses instead on the assignments God places in front of him. “If I’m here, I’m here to do work. I’m here to be a vessel.” “This is not about careers or jobs,” Boyd says. “This is about assignment level, and assignments are different when they’re God-led and God-ordained. If I’m here, I’m here to do work. I’m here to be a vessel.” The timing of Boyd’s latest degree carried special meaning because graduation came shortly after his oldest son graduated from high school. For Boyd, the connection between the two milestones was profound. A father of three, Boyd is quick to celebrate his children’s accomplishments. At the time of the interview, his oldest son had graduated from high school with a 4.3 GPA and was preparing to attend the University of Kansas. His daughter had earned academic honors and all-state recognition in flag football, and his youngest son was thriving in school and learning baseball. His wife has also been a driving force in their family while building her own career of more than 20 years in law enforcement. “I could have quit when they told me that college was not an option. I could have quit when they told me that getting a master’s degree probably wouldn’t happen. It’s about resilience.” When his children look at his journey, Boyd hopes they see resilience. “I could have quit when they told me that college was not an option,” Boyd says. “I could have quit when they told me that getting a master’s degree probably wouldn’t happen. It’s about resilience.” He knows they will see the diplomas and awards hanging on his office wall. But he also wants them to understand what it took to get there: academic struggles, losses, major life changes, doubts, and the daily choice to keep moving forward. “I’m going to leave a legacy that’s going to be worthy of following.” Boyd speaks specifically about wanting his oldest son to see that moving to Minnesota did not mean he stopped pursuing growth. “I chose to show him that I’m not going to quit on life,” Boyd says. “I’m going to go and be successful. I’m going to leave a legacy that’s going to be worthy of following.” That commitment also shapes the way Boyd serves others. He makes himself available as a mentor and thought partner because he remembers the people who invested in him. Teachers, relatives, coaches, pastors, faculty, and advisors all helped him move forward at different points in his life. “Somebody came back and helped me,” he says. “I’m always looking to help and to give back.” Boyd’s relationship with Bethel did not end when he completed a degree. He describes the university as a place where relationships helped him grow academically, professionally, personally, and spiritually. That experience shaped his view of what it means to belong to the Bethel community. “You’re going to be surrounded by folks who want to see you grow in all areas of life, and it’s not just for that moment; it’s for a lifetime.” Boyd says Bethel gave him the opportunity to establish a new foundation in his faith while learning alongside people who wanted to see him succeed. “You’re going to experience a rebirth,” he says. “You’re going to establish a new life and a new foundation in Christ, and you’re going to understand you’re going to be surrounded by folks who want to see you grow in all areas of life, and it’s not just for that moment; it’s for a lifetime.” For someone who spent years questioning whether he was capable of succeeding in higher education, that sense of belonging carries lasting meaning. Boyd now has two Bethel graduate degrees, a vocation focused on serving others, and a story he hopes will encourage his children and the people he mentors to keep going when the path ahead looks uncertain. His goal is no longer to prove that other people were wrong about him. It is to use what he has learned, continue following where God leads, and leave a legacy worth following.
